parts.text: Paul greets the Galatian churches as an apostle appointed through Jesus Christ and the Father, not through human authority. Christ gave himself for their sins to deliver them from the present evil world. Paul is astonished that they are turning from grace toward a distorted gospel. Even an apostle or heavenly angel must be rejected if preaching contrary to what they received. His allegiance is to Christ, not to pleasing people.

Paul explains that his gospel came by Jesus Christ’s revelation rather than human instruction. Formerly zealous for ancestral traditions, he persecuted God’s church, but God called him by grace to reveal his Son and send him among the nations. He did not immediately consult Jerusalem’s apostles; he went to Arabia and Damascus, later visiting Peter and James. The Judean churches knew him chiefly by the report that their former persecutor now preached the faith, and glorified God.

chapters.title: Gospel freedom and justification by faith

parts.text: Paul recounts a later Jerusalem visit with Barnabas and Titus. He presented his gospel privately, resisted false brethren seeking to impose bondage, and did not allow Titus, a Greek, to be compelled to circumcision. The recognized leaders added nothing to his message. Seeing God’s grace and his mission to the Gentiles alongside Peter’s to the circumcision, James, Cephas, and John offered fellowship, asking only that he remember the poor.

At Antioch, Paul publicly opposed Peter for withdrawing from Gentile meals out of fear, drawing others into hypocrisy. Such conduct contradicted the gospel: justification comes through faith in Jesus Christ, not works of the law. Paul describes himself as crucified with Christ yet living through Christ within him, by faith in the Son who loved and gave himself for him. If righteousness came through law, Christ’s death would be in vain.

chapters.title: The promise, the law, and Abraham’s heirs

parts.text: Paul asks whether the Galatians received the Spirit through law-keeping or hearing with faith. Having begun in the Spirit, they cannot reach completion through the flesh. Abraham believed God and was counted righteous; people of faith share his blessing. Reliance on law places people under its curse for failing to do everything it commands. Christ redeemed them from that curse by becoming a curse on the tree, opening Abraham’s blessing and the promised Spirit to Gentiles through faith.

God’s promise to Abraham and his seed, identified as Christ, is not canceled by the law given 430 years later. The law was added because of transgressions until the promised seed came; it could expose sin but not give life. It served as a schoolmaster leading to Christ and justification by faith. In Christ, believers are God’s children and one across distinctions of ethnicity, status, and sex, becoming Abraham’s seed and heirs of the promise.

Paul compares an immature heir under guardians with God’s people before their appointed freedom. At the fullness of time, God sent his Son under the law to redeem those under it and grant adoption. The Spirit of the Son enables them to call God Father, and they are heirs rather than servants. Paul fears their return to bondage through observances and recalls their former loving welcome. He warns that rival teachers seek their allegiance and longs for Christ to be formed in them.

Paul explicitly presents Abraham’s sons by the bondwoman and freewoman as an allegory of two covenants. Agar corresponds to Sinai and the present Jerusalem in bondage, while Jerusalem above is free. Like Isaac, the believers are children of promise, although those born according to the flesh persecute them. Citing the bondwoman’s exclusion from the inheritance, Paul concludes that they belong to the freewoman.

Paul urges the Galatians to stand in Christ’s freedom. Taking circumcision as the route to justification obligates them to the whole law and abandons grace. What counts in Christ is faith working through love, not circumcision or its absence. He rebukes those hindering their obedience and warns that their teaching spreads like leaven. Freedom must not become an excuse for the flesh; believers should serve one another in love, fulfilling the command to love one’s neighbour rather than devouring each other.

Walking in the Spirit opposes the flesh’s desires. Paul lists the flesh’s works, including sexual immorality, idolatry, hatred, division, and drunkenness, warning that those practicing them will not inherit God’s kingdom. The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance. Those belonging to Christ have crucified fleshly passions and should walk consistently with the Spirit, rejecting vanity and envy.

chapters.title: Bearing burdens and boasting in the cross

parts.text: Paul tells spiritual believers to restore someone caught in a fault gently, remembering their own vulnerability. They should bear one another’s burdens while examining their own work and accepting personal responsibility. Those taught should support their teachers. God is not mocked: sowing to the flesh brings corruption, while sowing to the Spirit brings everlasting life. Believers must not tire of doing good, but use every opportunity to help others, especially fellow believers.

Writing in his own hand, Paul exposes the circumcision advocates’ desire for outward display and escape from persecution. They seek to boast in the Galatians’ flesh without themselves keeping the law. Paul boasts only in Christ’s cross, through which his relation to the world has changed. What matters is a new creation. He pronounces peace and mercy, points to the marks of Jesus borne in his body, and closes with grace.
